developments.title: Inkling 2 Mini model released for Linux via Ollama 0.40.18
detail: Inkling 2 Mini, a 26‑billion‑parameter model, is now available on Linux (and Windows) through Ollama version 0.40.18.
It runs on devices with 32 GB of unified memory or more and includes performance improvements on macOS via custom kernels.
developments.why_it_matters: You can now run the 26B Inkling 2 Mini model locally on Linux systems with 32 GB RAM, enabling offline agentic coding without cloud services.

developments.title: Dutch Institute of Vulnerability Disclosure publishes full forensic report on ARTEX hack of its own network
detail: The Dutch Institute of Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD) has released the full forensic report on the September hack of its own network, an intrusion carried out using ARTEX, as reported by security journalist Kim Zetter. The forensic timeline shows the attack took only 1.3 seconds to hijack an administrator account and 20 minutes to take full control of the server.
Daniel Miessler shared the report while framing the sequence as a fully automated attack from start to finish.
developments.why_it_matters: Defenders can now read the public forensic report to see exactly how an automated ARTEX chain went from admin hijack to full server control in 20 minutes.

developments.title: ShellBench benchmark released for evaluating AI agents
detail: ShellBench, a new benchmark of 100 real-world tasks, has been released, testing 12 AI models across five harnesses with more than 53,000 graded runs. The release was announced by OpenClaw and ParseWaveAI, highlighting collaborative effort on the benchmark.
Initial results show a top score of 62.5% and a failure rate of roughly 40% on everyday tasks, with open‑source harnesses holding their own against proprietary counterparts.
developments.why_it_matters: The benchmark provides a standardized metric, letting developers compare agent performance and target specific improvements.

developments.title: Sakana Marlin update adds Twilight 2.0, Midnight 2.0, and refreshed slide output
detail: Sakana Marlin has been updated with Twilight 2.0, Midnight 2.0, and refreshed slide output.
Sakana AI says Twilight 2.0 supports quick, multi-angle examination, while Midnight 2.0 supports broad exploration for new findings.
developments.why_it_matters: Readers can use Sakana Marlin with its new Twilight 2.0 and Midnight 2.0 research modes and refreshed slide output.

developments.title: Qwen3.5-35B-A3B identified as Jev's latency backbone
detail: The quoted analysis profiled Jev across 9,984 prompts and found that Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, a mixture‑of‑experts model, most closely matches Jev’s throughput. The study also notes that Qwen’s tokenizer aligns better with Jev’s latency than Jev’s own token counts, and that Jev prefers Qwen over DeepSeek and Gemma.
developments.why_it_matters: Prioritizing Qwen3.5-35B-A3B can reduce inference latency for Jev‑based workloads, enabling faster response times without extra tuning.

developments.title: AVB's always-on agent tutorial uses a Tailscale-only private site on Hetzner
detail: AVB has been building an end-to-end always-on agent tutorial, and says its best feature so far is maintaining a private website through Tailscale. The pages are hosted on the Hetzner server where the agent service runs and are served over Tailscale, so only AVB's own devices can open them.

The site is used for studying new articles, learning new concepts, and daily personal newsletters, and AVB separately recommends taking time to learn Tailscale for homelab and private-knowledge-base setups.
developments.why_it_matters: Readers can adapt the same Tailscale-only Hetzner hosting pattern to keep an always-on agent's notes and newsletters private to their own devices.

developments.title: Ant Ling's Ling-3.2-air quantized to W4A16 outperforms Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and other Flash models
detail: The 120.4 GiB FP8‑only Ling‑3.2‑air model was quantized to a 72.5 GiB W4A16 version using INT4 for routed‑expert matrices, fitting entirely in 96 GB VRAM.

On a 4×RTX 3090 rig the quantized model achieves 4.1‑5.3 k tok/s prefill and 95‑105 tok/s decode up to 250 K context, beating Qwen3.8‑Flash‑Next, DeepSeek‑V4.1‑Flash, GLM‑5.3‑Flash, and MiniMax‑M3.1‑Flash.
Evaluation on GSM8K (97.04 % accuracy) and benchmarks like Terminal‑Bench 4.0, AutomationBench‑AA, and SkillsBench show quality comparable to or better than the original FP8 model.
developments.why_it_matters: You can download the W4A16 quantized Ling‑3.2‑air from Hugging Face to run faster local inference without resorting to 2‑bit quantization.

developments.title: Maziyar Panahi's single weighed-plate example cuts open-model carb-estimation error from 10.2 g to 7.8 g
detail: Maziyar Panahi tested open models on carbohydrate estimation: after showing one model a single food plate with its real weights, he asked it to estimate the carbs on 506 more plates. The model's average miss fell from 10.2 g to 7.8 g, roughly a 24 percent reduction in average error from one example.

Panahi reports that the other open models he tried also got better with the same approach. The gain comes from an in-context measured example rather than any retraining, according to his description of the experiment.
developments.why_it_matters: Anyone estimating carbs from plate images with open models can add one weighed-plate example, a prompt-only change that shaved average error by about 24 percent.

developments.title: HungerG AI harness outperforms DeepSeek V4.1 Flash in token efficiency and speed
detail: In a head‑to‑head test on four live 60 fps Three.js worlds, HungerG generated 3.1× fewer total tokens (402 K vs 1.25 M) and ran at 113 tok/s versus DeepSeek’s 55 tok/s, delivering cleaner lighting and geometry.

The comparison also showed HungerG used 4.9× fewer reasoning tokens and completed the runs 1.8× faster overall, and both models are available for free trial this week (HungerG on OpenCode Go and Qoder until Nov 30).
developments.why_it_matters: You can test the more token‑efficient HungerG harness for free, cutting inference costs and speeding up Three.js visualizations.

developments.title: Devin includes a free SWE model with quickly resetting limits
detail: The quoted post says Devin includes free SWE access, currently using SWE-2, as part of its subscription offering.
The quoting author says they frequently use SWE 2.1 and that its usage limits reset quickly.
developments.why_it_matters: Developers evaluating Devin can account for its included free SWE tier and quickly resetting limits alongside paid frontier-model options.

developments.title: Matt Van Horn compares 16 agent browser and computer-use tools on Apple Silicon
detail: Van Horn tested 16 agent browser and computer-use tools on an Apple Silicon Mac for T3 Code agents. Ardia Browser and OpenCode Browse beat agent-browser and Stagehand on speed, RAM, and tokens despite much lower star counts, while TryCua underpinned five of the tested stacks.

For a full switch, Ardia Browser plus TryCua offered 396 ms warm loads, no Chrome debugging popups or infobar, prompt-injection fences, and 1Password with Touch ID Passkeys. For staying in Chrome, OpenCode Browse plus TryCua used 18 MB RAM and cut page snapshots 53x versus Stagehand and 5x versus agent-browser; cua-driver used 27 MB RAM with zero focus steal (597 ms on Messages, 129 ms on Electron), using 8x less RAM than older Mac tools.

Boat booted four Ubuntu VMs in 1.9 seconds median for $0.001, and Codex Terra's native browser failed inside T3 Code because its host pipe existed only in the Codex desktop app. Separately, an MIT and reatools approach reverse-engineered desktop binaries into MCPs and made FreeCAD 55x faster with 35x fewer tokens, while staying in Chrome left a temporary debugging bar that one launch flag or Ardia Browser natively hid.
developments.why_it_matters: Developers can choose an agent browser stack from measured warm-load, RAM, snapshot, secret, and isolation tradeoffs instead of star counts.

developments.title: The Agentic Scientist framework automates coding‑agent research loops
detail: The Agentic Scientist introduces a meta‑controller that runs parallel coding agents through task drafting, ideation, planning, sandboxed experiments, analysis, and writing, with rubric‑based evaluation.
In early tests the system raised Doc‑to‑LoRA multi‑needle retrieval accuracy from 52 % to 98 % and produced a learned evolution strategy that outperformed CMA‑ES on unseen tasks.
developments.why_it_matters: Scientists can now let autonomous coding agents run full experiment cycles, cutting manual effort and boosting retrieval performance to near‑perfect levels.

developments.title: Plato's Key lets independently trained LLMs use each other’s representations after one rotation
detail: Vivien Cheng and collaborators introduced Plato's Key, a method for cross-model representation reuse. A single rotation lets independently trained LLMs use each other’s representations as their own, without gradients.

The announcement names Jerry Liu, Morris Yau, and HazyResearch as collaborators. The quoted source is embedded in a post that separately argues models are becoming commodities under the platonic representation hypothesis.
developments.why_it_matters: Practitioners can use Plato's Key to move representations between independently trained LLMs without gradient fine-tuning.

developments.title: Alexey Fateev's Colab launcher runs GLM-5.3-Flash Uncensored on RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell
detail: Alexey Fateev published a launcher that starts GLM-5.3-Flash Uncensored, a 321B model, on a Google Colab G4 instance with an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell 96 GB GPU and 176 GB RAM, then exposes a local API endpoint over SSH port forwarding to 127.0.0.1:18100 with OpenAI and Anthropic-compatible routes. It supports tool calls, thinking, vision, and reportedly zero refusals; the printed output includes the URL, model ID, and snippets for Claude Code, Codex, or OpenCode.

The default 2.51 bpw build occupies 98.1 GiB at 131K context and reportedly decodes 102.3 tokens/s with 1,190/2,255 tokens/s prefill, while 262K context, 3.05 bpw, and 4.05 bpw variants are listed at 98.9, 89.0, and 71.8 tokens/s decode. Colab compute units are included in Google AI plans and the G4 instance costs 10.05 units per hour, giving roughly 20 hours on the $20 Pro plan, 99 on the $100 Ultra 5x plan, and 199 on the $200 Ultra 20x plan.
developments.why_it_matters: Readers with Google AI subscriptions can run a 321B uncensored coding model locally through an on-subscription Colab instance instead of paying separately for Blackwell-class GPUs.

developments.title: Kody – Open‑source cloud for AI agents
detail: Kody is an open‑source platform that provides a cloud‑based store for agent memory, credentials, code, and automations, making them portable across any agent that integrates with the service.
The project is highlighted as a novel extension of the codemode/MCP work by Kent C. Dodds and the Kody team, offering self‑hosted capabilities without vendor lock‑in.
developments.why_it_matters: Developers can securely self‑host agent state and reuse it across projects, eliminating reliance on proprietary cloud services.

developments.title: Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Neon hand-wrote raw x86-64 Qwen3-0.6B inference engines
detail: Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Neon each generated a Qwen3-0.6B inference engine as raw x86-64 machine code in isolated sandboxes without compilers, assemblers, or mnemonic converters. Claude Opus 5.5 finished in 65 minutes with a 7,331-byte static ELF64 using f32 activations, transparent hugepages, and CCX pinning, reaching 21.44 to 125.13 tokens/s and beating llama.cpp by +10.4% to +28.9% across 1 to 40 threads for $21.40 across 175 turns.

Gemini 4 Neon finished in 103 minutes with a 10,752-byte binary, switching from int8 to a per-block Q15 (int16) AVX2 dot kernel after a near-missed token, pinning 15 weight layers (239.2 MiB) in a 256 MiB L3 cache with hybrid prefetcht0 and prefetchnta, and routing threads around an offline CPU core. It reached 22.27 to 188.35 tokens/s mean, peaking at 188.93 tokens/s at 32 threads versus llama.cpp's 103.82 tokens/s, for $16.72 across 90 turns.
developments.why_it_matters: The reported byte sizes and costs give a concrete baseline for evaluating agent-written low-level inference code under isolated, compiler-free constraints.

developments.title: Solidcraft Rust‑based Agent‑Native Development Framework
detail: Solidcraft, a pure‑Rust, MIT‑licensed project, made its first commit on October 8 and is already usable for building AI‑agent native applications.
The repository shows an acceleration of roughly 6.600 commits per week, indicating rapid development and extensive process tooling built directly into the code base.
developments.why_it_matters: You can now prototype agent‑native software with a fast‑moving, open‑source Rust framework, reducing the effort required to set up custom tooling.

developments.title: Radius introduces Pi-native control plane and gateway for agent workloads
detail: Radius offers a Pi-native control plane and gateway designed for managing agent workloads. The platform enables developers to run and coordinate agents directly on Raspberry Pi hardware.
It provides a lightweight interface for deploying, monitoring, and scaling agents without relying on external cloud services.
developments.why_it_matters: You can locally orchestrate AI agents on Raspberry Pi, cutting latency and cloud costs.

developments.title: Project Maya 1.1.82 adds Ling‑3.2‑air support and MTP‑accelerated decoding on NVIDIA GPUs
detail: Project Maya version 1.1.82 introduces native support for the 120.4 GiB Ling‑3.2‑air model, including official GGUF quantized weights (Maya‑S, Maya‑M, Maya‑L) that reduce disk and VRAM requirements. The engine also adds a built‑in MTP draft layer, adaptive per‑expert VRAM caching, CUDA graphs and double‑buffered DMA overlap for faster inference.

Benchmarks on a single RTX 3090 report 104.5 tokens/s decode with MTP (89.1 without) and 78.8 tokens/s at full 262 K context in INT8 KV; two GPUs reach 128.8 tokens/s peak decode and 102 tokens/s at full context. A 4‑GPU rig fits the largest Maya‑L quant fully in VRAM, enabling 100+ tokens/s without cloud services.
developments.why_it_matters: You can now run the 120 GB Ling‑3.2‑air model locally at >100 tokens/s on a single RTX 3090, removing the need for expensive cloud inference.
